query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidation annealing generates a controlled, nanocrystalline oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating that acts as a lubricious, wear‐stabilizing barrier at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation thermal annealing step to induce controlled surface oxide formation before exposing the coating to high-temperature wear.
generation.conditions: Testing performed at approximately 600°C (±50°C) under high-contact pressures of 1–10 GPa in an oxidizing (air) atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: A self-limiting, nanocrystalline oxide layer that adheres firmly to the coating, modulating surface interactions.
generation.mechanism: The formation of this oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and friction by acting as a lubricious, protective barrier. Its nanocrystalline structure helps accommodate strain and prevents further deleterious oxidation under high thermal and mechanical loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a notably lower wear volume and reduced coefficient of friction during high-temperature wear tests, with in situ surface analyses confirming a continuous and stable oxide film.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating in the as-deposited condition with no pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature wear conditions (~600°C ±50°C) with high-contact pressures (1–10 GPa) in an oxidizing environment; its validity outside this regime (e.g., lower temperatures or inert atmospheres) is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxide composition, layer thickness, and quantitative effects on wear rate are not fully established, and the optimal annealing parameters require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one set remains as-deposited (baseline) and the other undergoes a pre-oxidation annealing treatment at ~600°C designed to form a controlled oxide layer. Subject both sets to high-temperature wear tests at 600°C under contact pressures of 1–10 GPa in an air atmosphere.
measurements: Wear rate (via volume loss or mass loss measurements)
Surface and oxide layer characterization (using SEM and XPS) to evaluate the formation, continuity, and stability of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction coefficient or fail to form a stable, continuous oxide layer compared to the as-deposited baseline, then the hypothesis that the controlled oxide layer enhances wear resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . chosen.why: This experimental intervention directly fills the identified gap by investigating the overall wear response of FeNiCrCoCu coatings across an extended thermal regime. By comparing a baseline (as-deposited) coating with one that undergoes pre-oxidation annealing, the study tests the mechanistic hypothesis that a dynamically established, nanocrystalline, lubricious oxide layer governs wear resistance at high temperatures. The approach builds on prior evidence of composition-driven wear behavior at room temperature while removing previous limitations in the thermal scope.
